newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Trade ministers fight over infotech, labour rights.
newsitem.headline: Trade ministers fight over infotech, labour rights.

text.p: Trade ministers resumed intensive talks on Wednesday aimed at cutting tariffs on information technology goods and reconciling deep-seated differences over workers' rights.

Negotiators from the United States and the European Union scheduled another round of meetings to put the finishing touches to an outline Information Technology Agreement (ITA) thrashed out during four closed-door sessions on Tuesday.

A deal to free up trade in the $600 billion market for computers, software chips and other high-technology products by the year 2000 would be an important symbolic achievement for the first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

"There is no question that what the industrialised countries now hope for most here is a deal on information technology products and agreement to work hard for a basic telecommunications pact by February," said one key negotiator.

Ministers from the EU's 15 member states reviewed progress late on Tuesday with European Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, who negotiates on trade on their behalf, and asked him to clarify a number of points.

"We are still sorting through the European council's action. At this point it does not appear that there are any unsolvable problems presented by the council's action," Jay Ziegler, a spokesman for acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, said.
European officials said the queries raised by EU ministers covered the products to be included in the accord and the timetable for it to be phased in.
"There were some hesitations by some countries on specific points," Brittan's spokesman, Peter Guilford, told reporters. "But nobody implied they were backing away from an ITA."

Alongside efforts to iron out their differences, EU and U.S. officials were working hard to overcome reservations from other governments, notably in Asia, in the hope of achieving a "critical mass" of countries trading in information technology.

Progress on information technology was proving less elusive than on the contentious issue of whether the 128-nation WTO, set up in 1995 as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, should get involved in enforcing labour standards.

The United States, with strong backing from France and Norway, says that without action to tackle the exploitation of child labour and eradicate sweatshop conditions in the third world, support for free trade in rich countries will evaporate.

Diplomats said that Washington, digging in its heels, had repeated a threat to reject other parts of the meeting's final declaration to be published on Friday unless it won mention of the labour issue.

Poorer countries are equally adamant in rejecting a scrutiny role for the WTO. They say attempts to impose workplace rules is protectionism in disguise because the trade advantages their cheap labour gives them would be whittled away.

But WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero said he was confident a compromise could be reached. "We are making good progress, I am very encouraged," he told Reuters after late-night talks. "It's going a lot better than I expected."

WTO spokesman Keith Rockwell said labour was clearly the most divisive issue at the conference. But he said delegates were edging toward a consensus on textiles and agriculture and how the world trade body should tackle government procurement, investment rules and domestic competition policy.
"The atmosphere of the discussions has been positive and progress has been reported in a number of these areas," Rockwell said.
